verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon Lily of Testimony, a Miktam of David, to teach.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung to the tune called Lily of Testimony: a Miktam of David, set down to be taught.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is stage direction, not speech: the performers are told what tune to use and what the piece is for. The KJV counts the superscription as verse 0, so its 'verse 1' is our verse 3; the Hebrew treats it as part of the psalm, and so does this edition.

Three labels, none certain. 'Lily of Testimony' (shushan eduth) may be the opening line of a known song whose melody the choir already knew (Ibn Ezra), or an instrument shaped like a lily (Meiri, Metzudat Zion). 'Miktam' recurs in Psalms 16 and 56-60 and is unexplained; Rashi ties it to ketem, 'gold', and so to something precious, which Metzudat David follows. 'To teach' is unusual in a psalm title. It tells us this is a lesson to be learned by heart, and Ibn Ezra says the singers were commanded to recite it so the memory of God's help would not fade.

philological_notes.note: A psalm-title term of unknown meaning. Rashi links it to ketem 'gold' (Song 5:11), a precious thing; the LXX and later tradition guessed 'inscription'. Without agreement it stays untranslated in the dramatic layer.
The Piel infinitive 'to teach', rare in a title. It marks the psalm as a thing to be drilled, as with David's lament for Saul in 2 Sam 1:18, where the same verb is used.

verses.translation_literal: When he struggled with Aram-Naharaim and with Aram-Zobah, and Joab turned back and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was when David fought against Aram of the Two Rivers and Aram of Zobah, when Joab wheeled back from the northern war and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt: twelve thousand dead.
verses.directors_commentary:
The second half of the title sets the scene: a two-front war. David fights the Aramean kingdoms in the far north, along the Euphrates; meanwhile Edom, to the south, moves on the exposed country. Joab breaks off and turns back (vayyashov) to meet it, and the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea, is where Edom is struck. The verb 'struggled' (hatzoto) is rare and carries the sense of strife or quarrel: Rashi and Ibn Ezra note that the same root appears in Num 26:9, 'when they struggled against the LORD'.

The number is a famous problem. 2 Samuel 8:13 gives 18,000, to David, and says 'Aram' where this title says 'Edom'; 1 Chronicles 18:12 gives 18,000, to Abishai. The commentators harmonize: Abishai struck 6,000 first, Joab 12,000 after, 18,000 together (Rashi, Radak, Meiri), with David credited as the king in whose name the war was fought. The KJV smooths the verb to 'strove' and the numbers are untouched, but it makes the title one long run-on sentence with the first verse of the psalm. The Hebrew breaks it before 'O God'.

philological_notes.note: From נצה 'to strive', in the Hiphil infinitive with a suffix. The same form appears in Num 26:9 for the followers of Korah who 'struggled against the LORD'. A war is described as a quarrel.
The Valley of Salt, a place on the way to Edom, south of the Dead Sea; also named in 2 Sam 8:13 and 2 Kgs 14:7.

verses.translation_literal: O God, you have rejected us, you have broken out against us; you have been angry; you will restore to us.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, you have cast us off. You have burst through our walls. You have burned against us. Now turn, and bring us back.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with three accusations in a row, each a bare verb with no softening: 'you rejected us, you breached us, you were angry.' The people speak as a body, and they speak to God, not about him. Nothing is held back, and that is the register an actor should find: the grief of a nation that has just been broken and believes God did it.

'Broken out against' (paratzta) is the language of a city wall: a breach (peretz) through which an enemy pours. Metzudat David says exactly this: the war comes in from every side like a city whose wall has fallen. The KJV gives 'scattered', which is a different image; the ASV 'broken us down' is closer. The last verb, teshovev, from shuv, 'turn', is usually read as a plea ('turn us back'), and the KJV renders it as one: 'O turn thyself to us again.' Strictly the Hebrew is a second-person imperfect, a statement or a wish, not an imperative, and the commentators split on whether it asks or expects (Rashi, Radak: 'bring back your favour').

philological_notes.note: To breach, break through, as of a wall (peretz, 'a breach'). The image is of an enemy let in through a gap. The KJV 'scattered' loses the wall.
From af, 'nose, anger': to snort with anger. It belongs to the 'his nose burned' idiom and puns on af in the same breath.
A Polel from shuv 'to turn': 'bring back, restore'. It can be read as a plea or a hope, and the KJV picks the plea.

token_glosses.gloss: you have broken out against us

verses.translation_literal: You have made the earth quake, you have split it open; heal its fractures, for it is shaking.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have made the land shudder. You have split it open. Mend its wounds, for it is shaking still, and it is about to fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
The breach of verse 3 becomes an earthquake. The land of Israel is the body of the nation, and the war has torn it open like a field cracked by tremors. Ibn Ezra and Radak both read the quake as a figure: the loss of Israel's cities to the enemy felt like the earth shaking and splitting. Two words carry the verse: 'split open' (patzamtah), found only here, which Radak and Metzudat Zion take as splitting and cracking, and 'fractures' (sheveirehah), a word for a broken thing that also serves for a broken bone.

Then comes the turn, and the verb is medical: 'heal' (refah). Rashi notes that it is spelled with a final he though the root has an alef, and that many words do this; the sense is 'repair', as when Elijah 'repaired' the ruined altar of the LORD in 1 Kings 18:30 (Meiri). The KJV's 'broken it' for the rare verb flattens the image of cracks in the ground, and 'it shaketh' loses the sense, brought out by Radak, of a land about to fall unless God holds it up. The plea is practical: do not leave it half-broken.

philological_notes.note: A word found only here. Rashi glosses it 'you broke it', reports Moshe HaDarshan's 'tearing' (argued from the Targum's ופצים at Jer 22:14), and disputes only that proof: for him ופצים there means the fitting of a window frame. Radak and Metzudat Zion give 'splitting open'.
Imperative 'heal', spelled with a final he for alef. Meiri compares the repair of the broken altar in 1 Kings 18:30.

verses.translation_literal: You have made your people see a hard thing; you have made us drink wine of staggering.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have shown your people hardness. You have put a cup in our hands and made us drink it: wine that sends the whole nation reeling.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the quake to the cup. 'Wine of staggering' is the cup of divine wrath, a familiar image in the prophets (Isa 51:17, Jer 25:15): not a drink for pleasure but one that unsteadies the legs and clouds the mind, so that the drinker falls. The people do not drink it by choice; the verb is causative, 'you made us drink'. The picture follows the earthquake of verse 4: the land trembles, and the people on it stagger.

'Hard thing' (kashah) is a plain word, and the Hebrew keeps it plain. 'Astonishment' in the KJV is a guess from the root ra'al, which seems to mean 'reeling' or 'dizziness'; Rashi and Metzudat Zion tie it to a word for wrapping or dulling, as if the wine makes the heart numb. Radak and Meiri point out that the phrase is a short form for 'the wine of the cup of staggering'. The KJV 'astonishment' sounds mild. The ASV 'staggering' is closer to the physical effect.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun that appears with wine here and in Isa 51:17 and 51:22 with 'cup'. The root ra'al means 'to reel, to quiver'; Rashi connects it to wrapping or dulling (Nah 2:4), and Metzudat Zion to a word for blockage.
A Hiphil, 'you made us drink'. The people are given the cup, not taking it.

verses.translation_literal: You have given to those who fear you a standard, to be raised high, because of truth. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet you have given those who fear you a banner, a standard to be lifted high, for the sake of your truth. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
A shift in the middle of the lament. After the staggering cup comes a standard: nes, the pole with a banner on it that gathers an army or marks a rally point, as in Isa 11:12 or Exod 17:15, where Moses names his altar 'the LORD is my banner'. It is raised so that those who fear God can find each other and re-form after the rout.

The verse is built on a pun the KJV smooths. 'Standard' (nes) and 'to be raised' (lehitnoses) share a root; the Hebrew says, in effect, 'you gave a banner to be bannered'. The final phrase is read two ways. 'Because of truth' (qoshet) can mean that the standard is raised so that God's faithfulness stands out (Rashi, Radak, Meiri); some read it as 'bow' (qeshet), as the BBE does, so the verse becomes 'a place to flee from the bow'. The written text has qoshet, 'truth', with a tet and not a tav, so the KJV is on firmer ground. Rashi also reads nes as 'test' (nissayon), a trial to see who will stand firm; the pun allows both. 'Selah' is a pause mark, likely musical.

philological_notes.note: A banner or signal pole raised to rally troops. It is related to the verb in 'to be raised', and the verse puns on the root. Rashi also hears nissayon, 'test'.
'Truth, reliability', an Aramaic-flavoured word found in Prov 22:21. The BBE reads it as 'bow' (qeshet); the Hebrew text has the tet.

verses.translation_literal: So that your beloved ones may be rescued, save [with] your right hand and answer me.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that those you love may be drawn out of danger: save us with your right hand, and answer me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The petition proper. 'Your beloved' (yedidekha) is Israel as God's loved ones, a word with a family warmth. 'Rescued' (yechaltzun) has a physical picture: to be pulled out or drawn free, as Metzudat Zion's 'drawing out and removing' has it. The right hand is God's strong hand, the warrior's hand; Malbim ties it to wonders in war.

The last word is a Ketiv/Qere pair, and the versions split on it. The written text (Ketiv) is 'and answer us' (ועננו), the form the ASV and YLT follow, and the one Radak and Meiri comment on. The text as read (Qere) is 'and answer me' (וַעֲנֵנִי), the form the KJV, BBE and Rashi follow, and the one this edition translates. The two readings do not conflict: one voice, the king's, prays for all, and Rashi says that if God answers him, they will be rescued, because he fights for their sake.

philological_notes.note: Niphal 'be drawn out, be rescued', with a long ending of the jussive. Rashi glosses it 'be saved from evil'; Metzudat Zion ties the root to drawing out and removing.
Qere 'and answer me'; the Ketiv is ועננו 'and answer us'. Radak and Meiri comment on the written form, Rashi on the read form.

verses.translation_literal: God has spoken in his holiness: I will exult, I will divide up Shechem, and the Valley of Succoth I will measure off.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God answers. He has spoken out of his holiness: 'I will exult. I will carve up Shechem and take the measuring line to the Valley of Succoth.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer arrives as an oracle, and the voice changes: now it is God, or the king speaking for him, who says 'I'. 'In his holiness' is either 'in his sanctuary' or 'by his holy word', and the KJV's 'in his holiness' keeps both. The three verbs, 'I will exult, divide, measure', are those of a conqueror and a surveyor: a land is divided into allotments by a line, as in the days of Joshua.

The names matter. Shechem lies west of the Jordan in the hills of Ephraim; the Valley of Succoth lies east of it, in the Jordan plain. Together they stand for the heart of the north on both sides of the river, the old home of Jacob and then of the house of Joseph (Gen 33:17-18; Ibn Ezra, Meiri). Dividing and measuring them means that the land is again in Israel's hands. Radak adds that Abner had crowned Saul's son Ish-bosheth over the Gilead region, so the oracle claims all of Israel for the king. The KJV 'mete out' is archaic; the Hebrew is the plain 'I measure'.

philological_notes.note: 'I will exult', a cohortative: the victor's joy. Rashi reads it as joy in his deliverance.
'I will measure off', the surveyor's verb. It is paired with dividing (chalaq), the verb for allotting land by lot or line.

verses.translation_literal: Mine is Gilead and mine is Manasseh, and Ephraim is the protection of my head; Judah is my commander's staff.
verses.translation_dramatic: Gilead is mine. Manasseh is mine. Ephraim is the helmet on my head, and Judah is the staff in my hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The oracle lists the tribes like a king reviewing his realm. Gilead and Manasseh, both east of the Jordan, are named first with a doubled 'mine': the repetition is a claim. Then two images from a warrior's gear. Ephraim, the strongest northern tribe, is 'the protection of my head', a helmet; Judah, the tribe of the king, is the 'commander's staff', the ruler's rod. This is the picture of Gen 49:10, where Judah's mark is the staff that 'does not depart'.

The KJV 'lawgiver' is a legitimate reading of the participle (from 'to inscribe, decree'), and the ASV 'sceptre' another; the Hebrew word can name both the one who decrees and the staff he holds. Rashi reads it as 'my princes'. Ibn Ezra notes the geography: the house of Joseph in the north, Judah in the south. 'Strength of my head' in the KJV hides the picture of a helmet; the word ma'oz means a fortress or protection.

philological_notes.note: 'The protection of my head': ma'oz is a stronghold or defence, here applied to the head, so the image is of a helmet. The same phrase recurs in Ps 108:9.
A participle from 'to inscribe, decree': 'my lawgiver' or 'my commander's staff'. The word is used of Judah in Gen 49:10 and of a staff in Num 21:18.

verses.translation_literal: Moab is the pot of my washing; over Edom I throw my sandal; over me, Philistia, shout!
verses.translation_dramatic: Moab is my washbasin. On Edom I fling my sandal. And you, Philistia, raise your shout over me, if you dare.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three nations, three acts of contempt. Moab is a 'washing pot', a basin for rinsing the feet, the lowest household vessel; Radak says it is the bowl for dirty water, not the pot for cooking. Edom is the place where the speaker 'throws his sandal', a gesture of ownership and contempt, like Ruth 4:7 or the claiming of a field by treading it. The speaker treats Moab as a servant's tool and Edom as ground under his feet.

The third line is the riddle. 'Over me, Philistia, shout!' (alai pelesheth hitro'a'i) can be read as an invitation to cheer for the king, or, with a twist, as a taunt: Radak reads it as irony, 'shout if you can', and compares Psalm 108:10, which has 'over Philistia I shout'. The KJV 'triumph thou because of me' takes the first reading and loses the bite. The KJV 'cast out my shoe' also misses the point: the verb is simply 'throw'.

philological_notes.note: 'The pot of my washing', a basin for washing the feet or hands. Radak says it is not a cooking pot but the vessel for dirty water; Meiri reads it as a figure for utter subjection.
A Hithpael imperative feminine, 'raise a shout'. Radak reads it as irony and compares Ps 108:10, where the speaker shouts over Philistia.

verses.translation_literal: Who will bring me [to] a city of fortification? Who has led me as far as Edom?
verses.translation_dramatic: But who will bring me to the fortified city? Who has led me all the way to Edom?
verses.directors_commentary:
After the boasting, the doubts. The speaker looks at the hardest target, a walled city, and asks who can get him there. Rashi names the stronghold as Bozrah, in Edom, and Malbim follows. Radak and Meiri read the questions as looking back at the walled cities already taken from Philistia, Moab and Edom, and answer them: God did it. Either way the question is not for information; it expects the answer 'you, God', which the next verse will turn into an accusation.

The two verbs differ in tense, and the translations disagree. The KJV and BBE turn both into futures ('who will lead me into Edom?', 'who will be my guide'); the ASV and YLT keep the Hebrew perfect, 'who hath led me unto Edom?'. The Hebrew sets a need now (imperfect, 'will bring') against a guide in the past (perfect, 'has led'), and the contrast gives the verse its tension. 'City of fortification' is literal; Radak glosses it 'a fortified city', and Metzudat Zion says it is a stronghold too strong to take without a siege. The Aramaic Targum reads matzor as the city name Tyre ('to the ruined city of Tyre'), a different tradition.

philological_notes.note: A fortified city, literally 'a city of siege-works'. Radak glosses it 'a fortified city'; Metzudat Zion calls it a stronghold that cannot be taken without a siege. The Targum reads the word as Tyre.
A perfect, 'he has led me'. The KJV and BBE read it as a future; the ASV and YLT keep the past. Metzudat Zion glosses the root as guiding.

verses.translation_literal: Is it not you, O God, [who] have rejected us, and you do not go out, O God, with our armies?
verses.translation_dramatic: Is it not you, O God, who cast us off? You, O God, who no longer march out with our armies?
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to verse 11 is a question, and the question circles back to verse 3: 'you have rejected us' (zenachtanu), the same verb. The psalm has come full circle. The one who guides the king to Edom is the God who has rejected the nation and does not march with its armies. The 'O God' is said twice, one on each half, and an actor should lean on both: the speaker names the one he is accusing and the one he needs.

The KJV makes the first half a relative clause ('thou, O God, which hadst cast us off'), which the Hebrew does not have: it is a plain rhetorical question. 'Go out' (tetze) with the armies is the language of a divine warrior who leads his troops, as in Judges 5:4 or 2 Samuel 5:24. Ancient armies carried their gods and standards with them; Israel's God, by contrast, marches or stays at home as he chooses. The verse is an accusation and a confession at once: without him there is no army.

philological_notes.note: 'You go out with our armies': the language of a divine warrior who marches at the head of his host (Judg 5:4, 2 Sam 5:24). The verb is an imperfect, a repeated or continuing absence. The plural tziv'ot is the same root as 'hosts', as in 'LORD of hosts'.

verses.translation_literal: Give to us help from the adversary, and worthless [is] the deliverance of man.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give us help against the enemy. We have seen what the rescue of men is worth: breath, and nothing, a promise that will not bear weight.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn of the psalm, and it should be spoken by someone who has just been beaten. The opening word havah is an imperative with a rougher edge than the usual 'give': it is the word of 'Come now, let us...' (Gen 11:3), an urgent summons, so this is the cry of a people whose army has failed and who have only one court left to appeal to.

Then the line that strips human strength of its credit. Shav', 'emptiness, worthlessness', is the word used elsewhere for idols and for false oaths, so the speaker quietly puts human rescue among the things that cannot be relied on. Ibn Ezra reads the clause as aimed at our armies; Metzudat David says simply that human deliverance is shav' and has no use. The KJV is reasonable here, but 'vain' now mostly means 'conceited'; the Hebrew says the rescue is hollow. The KJV's 'from trouble' also blurs mitzar: the same consonants can mean the foe or the straits, so the word carries both a person and a predicament. The line sets teshu'ah, 'deliverance', against adam, the creature of the earth, so that human help is not merely weak but of the wrong order. Radak reads the first half as 'as you have helped us until now, help us from every trouble'.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of יָהַב 'give', a rarer verb than נתן, found mostly in the imperative and often as an urgent summons ('come, let us'). Here it is a sharp demand addressed to God.
A form ending in ת where one expects ה; Ibn Ezra takes the ת as standing for ה, and Radak says a ת can appear outside a construct chain.

'Emptiness, worthlessness'. Metzudat David says human deliverance is shav' and has no use; Ibn Ezra reads it as said against our armies. The word names idols and false oaths elsewhere (Ps 31:7, Exod 20:7), which is my own observation.

verses.translation_literal: In God we will do strength, and he, he will tread down our adversaries.
verses.translation_dramatic: In God we will fight with valor, and he himself, he alone, will come down on our enemies and trample them under his feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a note that no longer sounds beaten. The speakers do not say they will win; they say that in God they will 'do chayil', the idiom for acting with force and valor, which Metzudat David glosses 'we will do mighty deeds'. The noun chayil can also mean an army, and Radak takes it as force and host, so there is a play between 'we will act with valor' and 'we will be a force'.

The KJV's 'through God we shall do valiantly' reads well but turns be (in) into 'through', as though God were a tool, where the Hebrew puts the people inside him. The YLT's 'in God' is closer. The next clause is where the weight falls: ve-hu, 'and he, he himself', is an emphatic pronoun that takes the credit away from the army. The verb yavus, 'tread down', is physical and a little brutal, the stamp of boots on a crushed enemy; Rashi glosses it 'trample', and Radak compares the phrase 'trampling in the mud of the streets'. So the closing couplet reverses verse 13: human help is shav', but God's treading is real. Ibn Ezra hears prophecy here, a promise that victory will come at the end, and Meiri turns the speech into direct address to God ('you will tread down').

philological_notes.note: Strength, valor, and also a fighting force. 'Do chayil' is the idiom for acting valiantly. Metzudat Zion defines it as 'might and courage'; Radak takes it as force and host.
'Tread down, trample', a rare verb. Rashi glosses it 'trample'; Radak compares 'trampling in the mud of the streets'; Metzudat Zion calls it treading and trampling.
